title: When Is a Constant Compression Index Sufficient for Pile Downdrag? Joint Drag and Settlement Criteria with Laboratory and Field Checks
content: Checking maximum pile force can conceal relative uncertainty in drag because the head load dilutes its contribution. In 500 frozen synthetic cases, 29 of 105 joint total-force/settlement outer-envelope certificates at 10% are lost when drag increment replaces total force. We develop a procedure for deciding whether one constant compression coefficient meets both response tolerances. Ordered strain bounds are propagated through a finite-stiffness pile model with fixed monotone shaft and toe laws. Inverse-response intervals and a dimensionless tolerance-normalized index distinguish adequate simplification, insufficient information and incompatible response targets. A refined synthetic reference requires 16.124% minimum joint error; another case admits a 5.172% outer-envelope bound despite a 7.27 slope ratio. Nine published laboratory curves provide fit, shape and withheld-stress checks. AJOP reduces full-window and blocked RMSE relative to a constant logarithmic slope in all six Haihe specimens, while comparator and shape tests delimit that advantage. A Bangkok reconstruction tests transfer between monitored stages. The synthetic AJOP references are prescribed numerical benchmarks. The practical outcome is a shared admissible coefficient or a quantified reason to improve information or use a richer compression representation.
